Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Meet the Shape-Friends: Read-Aloud and First Encounter

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the four geometric shape-friends — Circle, Square, Triangle, and Rectangle — by drawing each on the board and asking students what they notice about each shape. Students share observations briefly.
Teacher reads the full prose story aloud from Textbook pp.25–33, using a different voice for each character. Students follow in their textbooks and listen for what each shape boasts about.

Teacher re-reads key boasting passages slowly; students echo each shape's claim aloud together (Circle: 'I am round and beautiful…', Square: 'I have four equal sides…', etc.). Teacher pauses after each character's speech to ask: 'What is this shape proud of?'

Students close their books. Teacher asks: 'Which shape do you think was right? Why?' Students share opinions in a brief open class exchange. Teacher closes by saying the story has a surprise answer — the shape-friends discovered it together.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the class's first encounter with the story, so the read-aloud should be expressive and unhurried — each shape's boast lands best when the voice changes distinctly. Students who are unsure which shape is which will benefit from the board sketches remaining visible throughout. No comprehension task is anchored today; the goal is enjoyment and the story's overall arc.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion: Who Said What and Why?

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — items 1–5 (pp.29): answer questions on the four friends and the story's events.

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to re-read pp.25–28 silently for two minutes, then asks: 'Who are the four friends in this story?' Students respond together. Teacher lists names on the board.

Teacher works through Let us think questions 1–4 (p.29) as a guided discussion — one question at a time. For each question, students think quietly, then a few share answers. Teacher confirms and clarifies using the story text.

Teacher introduces the True/False set (question 5, p.29). Teacher reads each statement aloud; students hold up a 'T' or 'F' slate (or show thumbs up/down). After each verdict, teacher asks one student to read the line from the story that proves the answer.

Teacher poses a brief closing reflection: 'Why do you think the four friends couldn't agree on who was the best?' Students share one-sentence responses. Teacher affirms varied answers and connects to the story's lesson.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may initially answer question 4 with a surface response like 'they stopped fighting'; guide them toward the idea that they learned every shape has its own value. For the True/False items, a common slip is claiming the square's sides are unequal — the text explicitly states four equal sides, so asking students to read that line aloud is the cleanest correction.
materials: Small slates or scrap paper for T/F responses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — items 6–7 (pp.29): talk about your friend and the shapes you see around you.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the first prompt (question 6, p.29): 'My friend is Meera. When she helps me, I feel happy and I can finish my work faster.' Teacher then pairs students and gives them time to tell each other about their own friend and what that friend helps them do.
Two or three pairs share with the class. Teacher prompts shy speakers: 'What game do you play together? What happens when your friend is absent?' Teacher affirms specific, detailed responses.

Teacher directs students to look around the classroom (question 7, p.29). Teacher models: 'The door is a rectangle. The clock face is a circle.' Students work in pairs, pointing to objects and naming the shape. Pairs report back: 'The window is a ___.' Teacher notes shapes on the board as they are named.

Teacher draws students together for a whole-class round: each student names one object-shape pair not yet on the board. Teacher connects back to the story — 'Just like in our story, every shape is useful in real life too.' A quick choral echo closes: students repeat each shape name with its key property.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 7 works best when students are genuinely scanning the room rather than recalling the story; prompt them to stand and point if it helps. If students struggle to name a shape's property alongside its name, model the sentence frame 'The ___ is a ___ because it has ___' before the pair activity.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.30): groups of 5 role-play the story, each student playing one character with actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher assigns roles and explains the activity (p.30): groups of five — Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, and Star. Teacher quickly demonstrates one shape's boast with an action (e.g., arms in a circle for Circle, hands on hips for Star's wise speech).
Groups scan the story in Textbook pp.25–33 to locate their character's lines. Teacher circulates, helping each group identify the relevant dialogue or narration for their shape.

Groups rehearse their role-play, reading lines aloud and adding actions. Teacher moves between groups, prompting louder voices, physical gestures, and emotional expression — 'How does Square feel when it boasts? Show that in your face!'

Two groups perform for the class. Audience watches for the moment the Star speaks and signals understanding by giving a thumbs-up. After each performance, teacher asks the class: 'What did the Star say that changed everything?' Students respond briefly.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often rush through the Star's lines because they are shorter; remind performers that the Star is the wisest character and should speak slowly and gently. If a group of exactly five is not possible, the narrator role can carry connecting lines between scenes so every student participates.

periods.activity_title: Articles 'a' and 'an': Hear the Difference, Fill the Blank

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.30): fill in blanks using 'a' with story-connected sentences.
Let us learn — B (p.31): fill in blanks using 'an' with sentences featuring vowel-starting nouns.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes on the board: 'Circle is ___ shape. Eagle is ___ bird.' Teacher reads both aloud and asks students which blank sounds right with 'a' and which with 'an'. Students experiment aloud. Teacher draws out the pattern: 'a' before consonant sounds, 'an' before vowel sounds.

Teacher works through Let us learn A (p.30) together as a class: reads each sentence aloud with a pause at the blank, students call out 'a', and teacher writes the answer. After all three sentences, teacher asks: 'What sound does each noun start with?' Students confirm: dog, cow, sparrow — all consonant sounds.

Teacher moves to Let us learn B (p.31): students work in pairs, reading each sentence aloud to hear whether the blank needs 'an', then writing the answer. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Say the next word — does it start with a, e, i, o, or u?' Pairs share answers; class confirms together.

Quick oral drill: teacher says a noun (eagle, dog, umbrella, star, apple, circle) and students call out 'a' or 'an' as fast as they can. Teacher includes nouns from the story (circle, square, triangle, rectangle) — students notice that 'a' fits all four and briefly explain why.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often apply 'an' by letter rather than by sound; the oral drill at the close is designed to surface this — if a student says 'an uniform' during the drill, use it as a class moment to model saying the word aloud before choosing. The story's four shape nouns make good drill material because they all begin with consonant sounds.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — C (p.31): choose 'a' or 'an' in mixed sentences and explain the choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes two columns on the board: 'vowel sounds' and 'consonant sounds'. Calls out ten nouns from everyday life; students sort them by calling out which column they belong to. Teacher confirms and briefly revisits the rule connecting column membership to the article choice.

Students open Textbook p.31 — Let us learn C. Teacher reads sentence 1 aloud: '___ brown hen laid ___ egg.' Students identify each blank independently, write their answers, then check by reading the filled sentence aloud to a partner. Repeat for sentences 2 and 3. Teacher takes whole-class answers and addresses any disagreement by asking students to say the noun aloud.

Teacher runs a short word-game: each student gets a slip of paper with one noun (or teacher calls nouns in a round). Each student must say a complete mini-sentence using 'a' or 'an' correctly — e.g., 'I saw an eagle.' The class gives a quiet thumbs-up or thumbs-down after each attempt. Teacher corrects and explains only when there is disagreement.

Pairs invent two sentences of their own — one using 'a' and one using 'an' — inspired by any object or character from the story (shapes, sweets, biscuits, the star). Each pair reads their sentences aloud. Teacher acknowledges correct usage and notes any recurring errors for a brief whole-class clarification.

periods.teacher_notes: Sentence 3 of Let us learn C contains three blanks in one sentence, which is the most demanding item in this set; if several students stall, model saying the sentence aloud blank by blank rather than reading it silently. Encouraging students to invent sentences from the story context (biscuits, the star, a circle) keeps the word work connected to the reading they have already done.
materials: Noun slips (or teacher calls nouns orally)

periods.activity_title: Writing About My Friend: Guided and Independent Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.32): fill in the friend-profile frame with personal details and complete 'My Friend' passage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the 'My Friend' frame from Let us write B (p.32) aloud, pausing at each blank. Teacher models filling in the frame for a made-up friend: 'My friend's name is Ravi. He is a boy. He is eight years old.' Students listen and note that every blank is personal — only they know the right answer for their friend.

Students think of one real friend and quietly decide their answers for each blank. Teacher circulates, asking individual students: 'Who is your friend? What does she like to play?' This warm-up makes the writing concrete before pen goes to paper.

Students fill in all six blanks in their textbook (p.32) independently. Teacher circulates and provides support: prompting students who are unsure of spellings to try sounding the word out, and affirming students who write with detail. Teacher does not correct spelling at this stage — fluency and personal detail are the goals.

Students pair up and read their completed 'My Friend' passage to each other. Each listener asks one follow-up question (e.g., 'What game does your friend like?'). Two or three students share with the whole class. Teacher celebrates diversity of friends and responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Task A of Let us write asks students to paste a picture of their friend — this requires a photograph brought from home and is better set as a take-home activity; it is not anchored in-class today. The guided frame in Task B gives strong enough support that most Grade III students can write independently once they have talked through their choices; resist the urge to pre-fill the board with model answers as it reduces the personal investment students bring to this task.

periods.activity_title: Draw the Shape-Friends and Build a Shape Picture

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.33): draw the four shape-friends from the story in the space provided.
Let us explore — A (p.33): draw an original picture using the four shapes, inspired by the cityscape illustration.

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws all four shapes on the board — circle, square, triangle, rectangle — naming each and noting its distinctive feature as students recall from the story: 'Circle has no corners. Square has four equal sides.' Students sketch the four shapes lightly in their notebooks as a warm-up.

Students open Textbook p.33 — Let us do A. They draw the four shape-friends in the space provided, giving each a face or personality touch if they wish (e.g., Circle smiling, Square looking proud). Teacher circulates and encourages careful shape formation — 'Is your square's sides all equal?'

Teacher directs students to the cityscape illustration on p.33 (Let us explore A) and asks them to look at how triangles become mountains, rectangles become buildings, and circles become the sun. Students then draw their own picture using all four shapes — it can be a scene from nature, a house, a vehicle, anything they imagine. Teacher encourages students to label each shape in their drawing.

Students hold up their shape pictures for a quick gallery share — teacher asks the class to spot each of the four shape-friends in a classmate's picture. One or two students describe their picture in a sentence: 'I drew a house with a rectangle body and a triangle roof and a circle sun.'

periods.teacher_notes: Both tasks share the same creative spirit, so running them back-to-back in one sitting works well — the first drawing warms up the hand and the second gives creative freedom. Encourage labelling during Let us explore A; it keeps the language connection alive even in a drawing task and gives students a gentle writing moment without a separate writing activity.

time_bands.activity: Revisiting the story: teacher asks students to tell the story of the four shape-friends in their own words without opening the textbook. Teacher accepts a chain retelling — each student adds one sentence. This surfaces how well students have internalised the narrative arc from boasting through conflict to the Star's wisdom.

Revisiting comprehension: teacher poses two or three spontaneous questions grounded in the story — 'What did Rectangle boast about? What did the Star tell the friends?' Students answer orally. Teacher invites brief disagreements and asks for the story line that settles them, keeping the discussion brisk.

Revisiting articles: teacher writes four blanks on the board — '___ circle, ___ eagle, ___ square, ___ umbrella' — and asks individual students to come up and fill each one. Class confirms each answer aloud. Teacher follows with a lightning round of five more nouns called out to the group.

Revisiting writing: students write two sentences in their notebook about their own friend — one sentence about what their friend looks like and one about what they do together — without using the textbook frame. Teacher affirms that these are their own words, not a fill-in.

Revisiting the shape drawing: students quickly sketch one shape-picture (any scene) on the back of their notebook page and whisper to a neighbour what shapes they used. Teacher closes by asking: 'The Star said all shapes together make the most beautiful pictures. Do you think the same is true about friends?' Students share one-word or one-sentence answers.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit revisits each spine the chapter built — the story retelling draws on the prose reading and oracy work, the article drill draws on the grammar work with 'a' and 'an', the two-sentence writing asks for fresh production rather than a repeat of the fill-in frame, and the shape sketch recalls the craft activity. No new content is introduced; the value is in students discovering how much they already know across everything the chapter covered.
materials: Textbook pp.25–33 (available for reference if needed)

items.source_context: Four arguing shape-friends — Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle — reconciled by a wise Star; themes of friendship, individual value, and collaboration.
items.item_stem: Read the sentences below. Write T if the sentence is true and F if it is false.

options.text: Circle boasts that it has no sharp edges and is round and beautiful.
In the end, the shapes decided that Rectangle was the best among them.
Square's four sides are of different lengths.
The four friends asked a star to help them settle their argument.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — T (Circle says it is round and beautiful with no sharp edges). 2 — F (Square's four sides are all equal in length). 3 — T (the friends agreed to ask the first person they met, who was a star). 4 — F (the Star told them they are all equal friends; no shape was declared the best).

items.source_lo: Student reads and demonstrates understanding of a prose story's characters, events, and key message using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Four arguing shape-friends — Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle — reconciled by a wise Star; themes of friendship, individual value, and collaboration.
items.item_stem: The Star told the four shape-friends something important. In 2–3 sentences, write what the Star said and what lesson the four friends learnt from it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Star gently reminded them that they are all friends and that together they can create the most beautiful pictures and patterns. She asked them to look around and notice that every shape has its own value. The four friends realised their mistake and promised never to fight again.

items.source_context: Talk about a real friend and classroom shapes; role-play the five characters (Circle, Square, Triangle, Rectangle, Star) from the story.
items.item_stem: Look around your classroom. Choose any two objects you can see and name the shape of each one. Which character from the story about the shape-friends would each object remind you of, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The clock is a circle — it reminds me of Circle because it is round with no sharp edges.

options.label: B
options.text: The clock is a triangle — it reminds me of Triangle because it has three corners.

options.label: C
options.text: The door is a circle — it reminds me of Circle because it is smooth.

options.label: D
options.text: The window is a triangle — it reminds me of Triangle because it stands tall.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may be confusing the shape of a clock with a triangle; they are applying 'corners' to a round object incorrectly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student has correctly identified the clock's shape but applied it to the door, suggesting confusion about which classroom object was named.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may be guessing based on tallness rather than on the shape's actual properties.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are playing the role of the Star in the story. Speak 3–4 sentences as the Star, telling the four shape-friends why each of them is special and why they should stay friends.

expected_elements: Names at least two shapes and their special quality.
Expresses the idea that all shapes are needed together.
Uses a gentle, wise tone fitting the Star's role.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: My best friend's name is ___ and he/she is ___ years old. His/Her favourite colour is ___ and he/she loves to play ___. (Accept any accurate personal detail the student provides.)

items.item_stem: Write 3–4 sentences about your best friend. Say who your friend is, what you both like to do together, and one thing that makes your friend special to you. Use your own words — do not use a fill-in frame.

expected_elements: Names the friend and gives one personal detail.
Describes a shared activity or game.
States one quality that makes the friend special.

items.item_stem: Fill in each blank with 'a' or 'an'.
items.visual_stimulus:
| # | Sentence |
|---|----------|
| 1 | Circle is ___ shape with no sharp edges. |
| 2 | The Star was ___ wise friend. |
| 3 | Triangle looks like ___ arrow pointing up. |
| 4 | Rectangle is ___ oblong shape with two long sides. |
| 5 | Square is ___ equal-sided shape that looks like ___ envelope. |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — a (shape begins with a consonant sound 'sh'). 2 — a (wise begins with a consonant sound 'w'). 3 — an (arrow begins with a vowel sound 'a'). 4 — an (oblong begins with a vowel sound 'o'). 5 — a (equal-sided begins with a vowel sound 'e' — accept 'an' here; 'an' envelope: envelope begins with a vowel sound 'e', so 'an').

items.item_stem: Say the following sentence aloud to your teacher and explain why you chose 'a' or 'an' in each blank: 'Rectangle found ___ orange biscuit and ___ square sweet at the shop.'

expected_elements: Explains the vowel/consonant sound rule in own words.
